title: M&A Attorney breaks down #1 Letter of Intent Mistake
content: If your letters of intent keep getting rejected from people selling accounting practices, there's probably a reason and it's probably that you're not answering a single question that they're all wanting you to answer. I'm Sarah Sharp. I help people buy and sell accounting practices nationwide. In doing that, I talk to about 21 different potential buyers of accounting practices every week. When I talk to those people, you get a lot of trends and one of the trends is a common theme I hear from people saying I've submitted 10 letters of intent and nobody has even responded. I can't seem to break through. I don't think it's the structure of the letter of intent and it isn't. It's not the substance. It's not usually the purchase price. It's that you're not answering the top most question on their mind. But before we get into that, if you find any content like this helpful, please a subscribe or comment, do all of that stuff with our video. Very, very much appreciated. If your letters of intent are constantly just being not even rejected sometimes but just flat out ignored, it's probably that you're not answering one of the biggest questions out there, which is how are you going to run the business? I know that sounds op-ed, but if you're buying an accounting practice and you're not paying attention to how much of the accounting practice is CPA work, so sort of find public accountant work, and you don't come with a plan for how you're going to take ownership of a CPA firm, especially if you're not a CPA, then they're not going to give you the time of day. No seller wants to talk to a buyer who doesn't have any plan for taking over a business that's so highly regulated. So let me back up and explain what I'm talking about. So not all accounting does not equal CPA. Those are different things. So there's a lot of accounting work and a lot of work that follows under the umbrella of accounting, like bookkeeping, payroll, general accounting, advice, even tax preparation is in the general accounting bucket. The CPA specific work is often referred to as a test work for audit and things like that where you can only do it if you have a CPA designation. So a lot of times people running their business and they are a CPA, they did go through all of the effort of getting that behind their name and getting that training, and so they're proud of it, sure, and then they start doing accounting work, all kinds of accounting work for different clients and they put CPA at the end of their firm because they think probably people care about that and they might as well. But when they go to sell, they might find all of these people coming through that have no CPA designation. And that's a problem because in most states in the United States and most jurisdictions even, and because it includes a Guam in Puerto Rico, you're not allowed to own a CPA firm unless you are a CPA. And so over half, I think it's 49 jurisdictions in the United States have a requirement that you have ownership of at least 51% or over half of the firm be owned by a CPA. There is one state, I think, of South Carolina that requires a higher requirement. So it's 66 and 2 thirds per set has to be owned by CPAs to run a CPA firm. So kind of like running a medical practice or any other highly regulated space, a regular Joe Schmo can't go in and own that business. Is this just dead to you then? You can't buy an accounting practice. So there's no reason and even proceeding and that's, you know, you've been beating your head against a wall this whole time. No, there's a lot of firms out there that are designated to be CPA firms that they don't really need to be because they don't do any audit or a test work. So when that happens, we just go through and restructure the seller firm to make it clear that it's not a CPA firm. Under the auspices of that regulatory body in the state, it's a general accounting firm. In general accounting firms can be run by all kinds of people, any kind of people. So you got to have a plan. You got to know if you're not a CPA and you're looking to buy a target, how much work do they do that is CPA specific or a test work? If it's a lot, then that's probably not the target for you. If it's just a little, there's a lot of solutions. You can leave that client list with the seller and say, I only want your non-a test work and everything else you can keep or I'm in a license with you to take. That's the simplest solution for a smaller deal. The larger acquirers and big companies that are doing a lot of rolling up, they take a more complex approach and they do what is often referred to as an alternative practice structure. So they'll roll in with an APS and say, I'm going to spin up small LLC that is going to be owned for sure, 51% by a CPA in every bit of audit or a test work is going to go into that LLC. Everything else goes into the general business. That LLC and I are going to have a license agreement where I basically siphon out all the profits. There's been really similar things done in the dental industry as well over the years when all of those are being rolled up in the 90s and early us. So it's a well-trodden path to compliance in that world. So you got to have a plan. You got to come in and say, you're a CPA firm, I'm not a CPA. In my letter of intent, I'm going to explain how this could even work. Even if you do that, prepare for a lot of pushback because these folks worked really hard on their designation. They think it's important. They want their clients to be well taken care of. So they're very, very suspicious of somebody who is industry agnostic and just looking at HVAC companies last month. They want to know that you've researched and know what you're getting into. So if you can confidently talk to them about the fact that in five different jurisdictions, you're not permitted to own a CPA firm. If you're not a CPA at all, even in the minority, and those are, you're wondering, Delaware, Hawaii, New York, the Northern Mariana Islands, and the Virgin Islands. So don't go look in there for a CPA firm unless you're a CPA. But if you can just confidently talk about the AI CPA, about CPA firm, about the fact that CPAs do things like audit and attest, but the other things are not considered to be CPA-specific work. If you can get really comfortable with those distinctions, you're going to go a whole lot further than going to a meeting with a seller and having them ask, what's your plan? You can't own a firm and you say, oh gosh, it so that's number one. The question that is on everyone's mind with their CPA and they're looking to letter of intent, they're going right to the signature page and they're seeing your designation, they're seeing you're not a CPA. What is your plan? Is it alternative practice structure? And it better not be, I'm going to hire a tax manager because we hear that all day long. Let's just say hiring is hard. If you don't already have talent identified, it's going to be a very long road to hoe and most of these sellers have gone through the process of trying to hire qualified talent and they are jaded. If that's your plan, they're going to be highly suspicious that that's not going to work out for you and the same way that it may not have worked out for them. Don't say I'm going to hire a tax manager to all your work because it's just easy widgets and any old accountant can do it. Don't say I plan on offshoring it. Say I recognize that you have CPA specific work. We're only interested in the general accounting work and we're going to either leave that with you or come up with a different solution and we have identified and already hired qualified talent or I have partnered with somebody who has qualified to do this work and submit these tax filings and we will take good care of your clients because at the end of the day, especially with the multiple that these are trading at and accounting, which is often not terribly different than what you would have made as a seller if you had just kept working through two and a half more years. Since they're trading at that whole pretty near just continuing to work multiple, usually the sellers are selling for one reason and that reason is because they want to take care of their clients. So if you aren't coming through with a letter of intent that explains how you're going to take care of their clients on its face, you're not going to get through the door. If you found this valuable, please subscribe and engage in some more content. Maybe somewhere in here, I should say, I'll talk more about what makes a good letter of intent in a winning offer in a different video. So make sure and link that below.
description:
If you're planning on buying an accounting practice, one of the most common questions that comes up is how to handle the letter of intent. In this video Sara Sharp reviews how to effectively write a letter of intent that sets you up for success in your transaction.

For more information on Deal Academy, a program that teaches you how to buy and sell accounting practices, click the link here:
https://www.dealacademy.org

To connect with Sara Sharp on LinkedIn:
https://www.linkedin.com/in/sara-sharp-9a2a98b/

For more information on our Mergers and Acquisitions law practice click here:
https://www.skandslegal.com
